items.paragraph: For much of the twentieth century, intensive care units kept families at a distance. items.paragraph: A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. items.paragraph: Memory researchers have repeatedly found that trying to recall material, for example by answering questions on it, fixes it in memory better than reading it again for the same amount of time. Students tend to resist the finding because rereading feels productive: the text grows familiar, and familiarity feels like knowing. Recall, by contrast, is effortful and exposes gaps, which feels like failure. The finding has limits that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Testing oneself helps most when the material has first been understood; quizzing a student on ideas that were never properly explained simply rehearses confusion. Recall is a way of strengthening learning, not a substitute for the teaching that makes something worth recalling.

items.paragraph: The idea of a keystone species, one whose removal brings an ecosystem's arch tumbling down, has been enormously useful in persuading people that a single unremarkable creature can matter far beyond its numbers. items.paragraph: Tipping looks the same everywhere, a small sum left for good service, but it does quite different work in different places. Where wages for service staff are set on the assumption that tips will make up the difference, a tip is not a bonus at all; withholding it cuts the worker's basic pay, and the customer who tips carefully according to service is in effect setting a stranger's wage. Where staff are paid a full wage, the tip really is a discretionary reward, and leaving little or nothing is an ordinary judgement rather than a harm. Visitors who carry their home habits abroad therefore often get it wrong in both directions: they may seem mean in one country and needlessly lavish in another, since the same gesture carries a different meaning depending on how pay is organised.

items.paragraph: A student who goes out the night before an important exam, or an athlete who skips training before a big race, may seem simply careless. Often something subtler is happening. By creating an obstacle in advance, the person secures an excuse: if they fail, the failure can be blamed on the late night rather than on a lack of ability, and if they succeed despite the handicap, their ability looks all the greater. The strategy protects a fragile sense of competence. Its price is that it makes failure more likely, and it tends to be adopted most by those who are least sure of their ability, the very people who could most use a fair test of it.
